On September 15th, as two NYPD officers sought to subdue a fare evader on the L Train in Brooklyn, nine shots were fired, leaving a police officer, a suspect, and two innocent bystanders wounded. Gregory Delpeche, 49 years old, an employee at Woodhull Hospital, was shot in the back of the head sustaining a serious brain injury, and 26-year-old Kerry Gahalal was left with a bullet lodged in her

This incident will alter the course of their lives forever, an unfortunate and irreversible outcome incurred due to negligence by those who were sworn to protect us. This tragedy results from a larger issue that demands our attention and decisive action. In response, I am introducing Introduction 1095, which mandates that any injury or death to a civilian caused by NYPD must be reported to the Civilian Complaint Review Board within 24 hours of the injury. We must address pervasive trends and the lack of training our officers receive, especially in deescalation of otherwise nonviolent situations. In risky interactions in our public spaces, we must set a precedent towards de-escalation as the norm and innocent bystanders will be protected. The public safety of New Yorkers should be our utmost priority, and those who protect us should be accountable for their actions while serving and protecting others. Access to permanent and stable housing is a key component of well-being, and too often people with criminal legal system involvement face increased barriers to securing this housing. With some incarceration stays interrupting chronicity requirements that really deters the facilitation of access to supportive housing.
